reason: This text presents a theological narrative centered on God's covenantal relationship with the Israelites based on faith and obedience rather than social status. The plagues affect all Egyptians—elite and common people—equally, including Pharaoh's household. The death of the firstborn explicitly strikes 'from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the slave girl behind the millstones,' demonstrating that vulnerability and death are not status-differentiated. The Passover ordinance applies universally to 'all the congregation of Israel' regardless of rank. Significantly, the chosen people are enslaved Hebrew slaves, not Egypt's elite. The text emphasizes divine selection based on covenant and obedience ('if you obey my voice'), not inherent superiority of any elite class. God's favor and protection are presented as theological/covenantal gifts, not as validation of inherent social hierarchy.
